identity.title: Data Scaling Laws in Imitation Learning for Robotic Manipulation

problem.claim: The paper investigates whether robotics, particularly robotic manipulation, exhibits data scaling laws and whether scaling can produce single-task policies that deploy zero-shot across same-category objects and environments.

contributions.claim: A comprehensive study of imitation-learning data scaling using variation in training environments, objects, and demonstrations.
Characterization of how environment, object, and demonstration diversity relate to policy generalization.
An efficient data-collection strategy based on the reported scaling findings.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present an empirical investigation of data scaling laws specifically for robotic manipulation and derive an efficient collection strategy from its findings.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that policy generalization follows a roughly power-law relationship with the number of training environments and objects.

The authors report that environment and object diversity matter more than the absolute demonstration count; beyond a threshold of demonstrations per environment or object, additional demonstrations have minimal effect.
The authors report collecting over 40,000 demonstrations and conducting more than 15,000 real-world robot rollouts under a rigorous evaluation protocol.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper asks whether data scaling laws transfer to robotic manipulation and support zero-shot deployment across novel objects and environments.
It varies the numbers of training environments, objects, and demonstrations while collecting data across many environments and objects.
Generalization approximately follows power laws for environments and objects, while diversity outweighs demonstration quantity after a per-environment or per-object threshold.
The authors propose efficient collection and report approximately 90% success on two tasks in novel environments with unseen objects using data collected by four collectors in one afternoon.

source_observation.claim: The abstract separates scaling dimensions—environments, objects, and demonstrations—and reports different effects for each, including a threshold beyond which more demonstrations have minimal impact.

lessons.interpretation: A paper can make a more actionable scaling claim by decomposing a total resource into distinct axes and identifying where marginal returns change.
lessons.application: When presenting a data-scaling study, report performance against each meaningful diversity or quantity axis separately, and state any observed saturation condition.
lessons.exception: This framing may be unsuitable when the data axes cannot be varied independently or when the abstract lacks evidence for a saturation pattern.

unknowns: The threshold for demonstrations per environment or object is not quantified.
The two tasks, policy architecture, task-specific data amounts, and success-rate uncertainty are unspecified.
The abstract does not detail the evaluation protocol or establish whether the reported relationships are statistically validated.
